scope: Read-only attribution of retained canonical scale SQLite allocation; no current database or actor/grader access.

measured.scopeLimit: One canonical SQLite file; WAL, media blobs, replay copies and total workspace are outside this measurement. dbstat unused is within allocated pages, not evidence of safely reclaimable bytes.

sourceEstablished.fact: Each ordinary schema index creates one generic entry per stored row, represented by four B-trees: base rowid table, primary-key autoindex, ordered covering lookup, and row cleanup. This repeats index keys and addresses; it does not copy the full application row body into every index.

String/Id/Bytes key encoding is a two-byte tag plus hexadecimal byte expansion (2N+2 ASCII bytes); integer keys occupy 22 ASCII bytes. Unused c0–c7 slots are SQL NULL. Raw table/index names and row IDs also occur in physical records.

Each search posting is held in three B-trees; the posting table is WITHOUT ROWID. For each row and derived index, there is one posting per distinct nonempty normalized word prefix node. A per-row set deduplicates repeated prefix nodes; the dictionary is shared within table/index.
Rows are persisted as typed canonical JSON text, including field names and value tags. In-memory Arc sharing is not on-disk row-body compression.
All tables receive byId. Each Count target adds its unique group index. Delivery log has byId plus three generated orderings; its receipt table has byId plus unique byRow.

A newly delivered message to R distinct recipients creates R log rows and R initial receipt rows: 6R ordinary logical index entries, represented by 24R generic B-tree records, before the source message, maintained groups, or search postings. At declared membership cap 50 this conditional example is 300 logical entries / 1200 generic records. Actual mean R and population share are unknown. Generated delivery rows carry metadata, not full message bodies.
Generated delivery IDs are 64-character hexadecimal SHA-256 digests. The ordinary byId key therefore encodes this ID as 130 characters, in addition to the separate raw row address.

The schema contains identical-column unique/nonunique index pairs for follows and reactions. Both names are stored separately; they have different declaration semantics and consumers have not been audited for safe consolidation.
Replacement reindexes only changed ordinary keys and skips retokenization when derived key components are unchanged; this source does not support a blanket every-update-rebuild allegation.

schemaInventory.method: static declaration scan plus frozen compiler materialization rules; no compiler or database execution
schemaInventory.interpretation: 35 schema table kinds share generic SQLite storage; these are not 35 separate application SQLite tables. 83 declarations are not 83 index entries per row; each row gets only its table indices. Count target population follows occupied groups, not source-row count.

conclusion: Confirmed structural storage amplification in the current generic representation, with implementation and authored-index consolidation opportunities. The evidence does not establish an irreducible 5.2 GB semantic requirement, nor a measured safely removable percentage or a correctness defect.
unknowns: Per-application-table and per-index cardinalities; delivery/receipt versus posts/follows share of the generic structures.
Key/ID length distributions and actual recipient fanout, message word-prefix counts, and maintained-group populations.
Which identical-column authored index names can be consolidated without changing program lookup selection or uniqueness.
Actual byte, read, write, deletion, migration and rebuild tradeoffs of compact keys or fewer physical structures.
Cause of the residual 4096 bytes outside the summed dbstat groups and freelist; immaterial to the dominant attribution.
smallestJustifiedFollowup: After grading, use a separately retained database copy and authorized metadata-only table/index counts plus key-length histograms to rank the measured contributors. Then consider one isolated representation comparison preserving ordering, uniqueness, row cleanup, index rebuild, search, authority and custody. No new ticket/design/implementation or savings claim is made here.
